blocks.title: Classifying Data: Qualitative vs. Quantitative
teacherCues: Write 'prices of used cars' and 'jersey numbers' on the board. Ask: 'Which can you do meaningful math with? Which are just labels?'
Present a list: telephone numbers, ages, lengths of videos, types of flowers. Let students classify each.

discoveryHook.scenario: Data comes in two flavors: numbers you can measure and compare (quantitative), and labels that put things into groups (qualitative). Knowing the type helps you choose the right graph and the right statistics.

explanation: [[kw:Qualitative data]] (or categorical data) consist of labels or nonnumerical entries that can be separated into categories. Operations like adding or finding a mean do not make sense.
[[kw:Quantitative data]] consist of numbers that represent counts or measurements. You can perform arithmetic operations and compute statistics.
Examples of qualitative: jersey numbers, zodiac signs, telephone numbers, car brands, eye color.
Examples of quantitative: prices, weights, lengths, ages, test scores.
Tip: If it makes sense to take an average of the data, it's quantitative. If averaging would be meaningless, it's qualitative.

rows.2: Numbers you can compare and average.
Labels; even though digits, they don't measure anything.

formulaCard.title: Data Types
notes: A frequency count can be shown for both types.
The type of data determines appropriate displays and measures.

examples.title: Example A – Identify the Data Type
examples.prompt: Classify each as qualitative or quantitative: (a) budgets of feature films, (b) file formats of documents.
steps: Budgets are numerical dollar amounts → quantitative.
File formats (PDF, DOCX) are categories → qualitative.

examples.title: Example B – Shoe Sizes vs. Street Addresses
examples.prompt: Shoe sizes are numbers like 8, 9.5, 10. Street addresses are numbers like 123 Main St. Which is quantitative?
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss with a partner: Why are shoe sizes quantitative even though they're often half‑sizes, but street addresses are qualitative?
steps: Shoe sizes are measurements of foot length; you can average them → quantitative.
Street addresses are labels for location; averaging them is nonsense → qualitative.

examples.title: Example C – Practice
examples.prompt: Classify: weights of bears, brands of cars.
steps: Weights are measured in pounds/kilograms → quantitative.
Car brands are categories (Ford, Toyota, etc.) → qualitative.

confusionCorner.title: Numbers Can Be Qualitative!
confusionCorner.body: Just because data are written as numbers doesn't make them quantitative. Zip codes, phone numbers, and jersey numbers are labels, not measurements.

questions.prompt: Data that consist of labels or nonnumerical categories are called ___ data.
Are the lengths of videos on a website qualitative or quantitative?
hints: They are measured in minutes or seconds.

questions.prompt: Are telephone numbers qualitative or quantitative?
hints: Can you meaningfully average phone numbers?

blocks.title: Choosing and Creating Appropriate Data Displays
teacherCues: Display the eye color survey frequency table. Ask: 'What type of data is this? What graph would show the parts of a whole?'
Then show the speed data for two interstates. 'This is quantitative. How can we compare the two groups?'

discoveryHook.scenario: The type of data — qualitative or quantitative — guides your choice of graph. Circle graphs and bar charts show categories; histograms, box plots, and line graphs show numerical data. Choosing the right display makes the story in the data clear.

explanation: The best data display depends on the type of data and what you want to show.
For [[kw:qualitative data]]: use circle graphs (pie charts) to show parts of a whole, or bar graphs to compare category frequencies.

For [[kw:quantitative data]]: use histograms or stem‑and‑leaf plots to show distributions; box‑and‑whisker plots to compare groups; line graphs to show change over time; scatter plots to show relationships.
Example: Eye colors are qualitative → circle graph shows proportions. Vehicle speeds are quantitative → double box‑and‑whisker plot compares two interstates.

formulaCard.title: Matching Data to Displays
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Qualitative} \rightarrow \text{Circle graph, Bar graph} $$ $$ \text{Quantitative} \rightarrow \text{Histogram, Box plot, Line graph, Scatter plot} $$
notes: Always label axes and provide a title.
Multiple displays can be appropriate; choose based on your message.

examples.title: Example A – Circle Graph for Eye Colors
examples.prompt: Eye color survey: brown 63, blue 37, hazel 25, green 10, gray 3, amber 2 out of 140 students. Create a circle graph.
steps: Find each fraction of the whole: Brown 63/140 = 0.45, Blue 37/140 ≈ 0.26, etc.
Multiply by 360° to get angle: Brown ≈ 162°, Blue ≈ 95°, Hazel ≈ 64°, Green ≈ 26°, Gray ≈ 8°, Amber ≈ 5°.
Draw a circle, use a protractor to mark angles, label sections.

examples.title: Example B – Double Box Plot for Speeds
examples.prompt: Vehicle speeds on two interstates are given. Create a double box‑and‑whisker plot to compare.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is a double box plot better than two separate histograms for comparing the interstates?
steps: Find the five‑number summary for each interstate.
Interstate A: Min 62, Q1 67, Median 69.5, Q3 75, Max 84.
Interstate B: Min 59, Q1 68, Median 72.5, Q3 79, Max 82.
Draw both plots on the same number line for comparison.

examples.title: Example C – Practice
examples.prompt: You have the number of students in a marching band each year from 2010 to 2020. What display would you choose?
steps: The data are quantitative and show change over time.
A line graph would clearly show trends from year to year.
A bar graph could also work, but a line graph emphasizes the trend.

confusionCorner.title: Not Every Display Fits Every Data Set
confusionCorner.body: Avoid using a circle graph for quantitative data or a line graph for categorical data. Always ask: 'Does this display make sense for this type of information?'

questions.prompt: A circle graph is most appropriate for displaying ___ data as parts of a whole.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Circle graphs are best for qualitative (categorical) data.

questions.prompt: What type of display is best for showing the distribution of test scores in a class? (histogram, circle graph, or line graph)
hints: You want to see how scores are spread out.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: A histogram shows the distribution of quantitative data.

questions.prompt: To compare the ages of two different groups, which display would you use? (double box‑and‑whisker plot, circle graph, or scatter plot)
hints: It shows medians and spreads side by side.
Box plots are great for comparing groups.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: A double box‑and‑whisker plot is ideal for comparing two groups.

blocks.title: Analyzing Misleading Graphs
teacherCues: Show a bar graph where the vertical axis starts at $15,500 instead of $0. Ask: 'Does this make the increase look bigger than it really is?'
Then show a graph with uneven intervals. Ask: 'Are the changes between years really that different?'

discoveryHook.scenario: Graphs can be manipulated to exaggerate or hide the truth. A scale that doesn't start at zero, uneven intervals, or missing labels can all mislead. Learning to spot these tricks makes you a smarter consumer of data.

explanation: A [[kw:misleading graph]] is a statistical graph that is not drawn appropriately, often to create a false impression.
Common ways graphs mislead:
• The vertical scale does not start at zero (exaggerates differences).
• The scale has uneven increments (distorts the rate of change).
• Bars or pictures are not proportional to the data.
• Labels, titles, or keys are missing, making interpretation difficult.
Always examine the axes, scale, and labels before drawing conclusions.

formulaCard.title: Questions to Detect Misleading Graphs
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Does the scale start at 0? Are increments even? Are axes labeled?} $$
notes: A break in the scale should be clearly indicated if the scale doesn't start at 0.
Check that bars, pictures, and areas are proportional to the numbers they represent.

examples.title: Example A – Tuition Graph
examples.prompt: A graph shows tuition rising from $15,500 to $17,000 over 4 years, but the vertical axis starts at $15,500. Why is it misleading?
steps: The scale starts at $15,500 instead of $0.
This makes the $1,500 increase appear much larger relative to the graph's height.
Someone might think tuition more than doubled, but it only increased by about 10%.

examples.title: Example B – Wage Graph
examples.prompt: A graph shows hourly wages from 2008–2013. The vertical scale goes from 8.90 to 9.06 with increments of 0.01. Why is this misleading?
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How would the graph look different if the scale started at $0 and used larger increments?
steps: The very small, uneven increments exaggerate tiny changes.
A change from $8.95 to $9.01 looks huge when each grid line is only 0.01 apart.
A properly scaled graph with $0 start would show wages as nearly flat.

examples.title: Example C – Practice
examples.prompt: Describe how a graph with bars of different widths but labeled with the same categories could be misleading.
steps: Wider bars appear more significant visually, even if their heights are proportional.
The viewer's eye is drawn to the larger area, distorting the perceived comparison.
All bars should have the same width for fair comparison.

confusionCorner.title: A Break in the Scale Is Not Always Misleading
confusionCorner.body: If a graph clearly shows a break (a zigzag or gap) near the bottom, it can be acceptable. The problem is when the scale starts above zero without any indication.

questions.prompt: A graph that exaggerates or distorts the data is called a ___ graph.
hints: It leads you to a false conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why is a graph with a vertical scale starting at 50 instead of 0 misleading? (Type one sentence)
questions.answer: It exaggerates differences between data values.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: It makes differences appear larger than they really are.

questions.prompt: What should you check first to see if a line graph is misleading? (Type one word, e.g., scale)
hints: Look at the numbers on the axes.
Is it even? Does it start at zero?

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Choose, Create, and Critique Data Displays
teacherCues: Summarize the decision process: 1) Classify the data (qualitative or quantitative). 2) Determine the purpose (compare, show distribution, show change). 3) Select the appropriate graph. 4) Create it accurately. 5) Critique for misleading elements.
Walk through the eye color survey: qualitative → purpose: parts of a whole → circle graph.

discoveryHook.scenario: With the blueprint for data displays, you can confidently present any data set: classify the data, pick the right graph, create it with proper scales and labels, and double‑check that it's honest. Good decisions start with clear, accurate visualizations.

explanation: 1. Understand: Classify the data as qualitative or quantitative. Identify the message you want to communicate.
2. Solve – Choose: Match the data type and purpose to a display type. Qualitative: circle graph, bar graph. Quantitative: histogram, box plot, line graph, scatter plot.
3. Solve – Create: Build the graph with accurate scales, clear labels, and a title. For circle graphs, compute angles. For box plots, find the five‑number summary.
4. Conclude – Critique: Check the graph for misleading elements: scale starting above zero, uneven intervals, missing labels. Redraw if necessary.

rows.1: Qualitative data, show parts of a whole

formulaCard.title: Data Display Blueprint
notes: Always start the scale at zero unless a break is clearly shown.
Label axes and include a title.

examples.title: Example A – Full Blueprint
examples.prompt: Use the blueprint to choose and create a display for the eye color survey data.
steps: Understand: Qualitative data on eye color from 140 students.
Choose: Circle graph shows proportions well.
Create: Compute angles, draw sections, label with color names and counts.
Critique: Title present, sections proportional, legend included. No misleading elements.

examples.title: Example B – Critique a Graph
examples.prompt: A bar graph shows sales rising from 99.5 to 104.5 million dollars, but the vertical axis starts at 99.5. Critique it.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: How would you redraw this graph to be honest?
steps: The scale starts at 99.5, exaggerating the $5 million increase.
Redraw with a scale starting at $0. The bars would be very tall at the bottom, and the increase would look much smaller.
Or, clearly show a break in the scale and label the axis appropriately.

examples.title: Example C – Practice
examples.prompt: You have average monthly precipitation (inches) for a city. Choose and justify a display.
steps: Quantitative data over time (months).
A line graph or a bar graph could show the pattern across months.
A line graph emphasizes the trend and seasonal changes.

confusionCorner.title: Honesty in Graphing
confusionCorner.body: A graph should make the data easier to understand, not harder. If a graph gives a false impression — even unintentionally — it's misleading. Always ask: 'Would the data look different if I changed the scale?'

questions.prompt: The first step in choosing a data display is to classify the data as qualitative or ___.
For qualitative data showing parts of a whole, which graph is most appropriate? (circle graph, histogram, or line graph)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: A circle graph (pie chart) is best for parts of a whole.

questions.prompt: Name one thing you should check to determine if a graph is misleading.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Check the scale, labels, and title.
